svg.text: Hardware map: the layers one memory access passes through
Blue = where it is covered (#N = Trading System Notes #N; MESI = the MESI topic post; Ref N.N = a section of the Reference page). Numbers are rough magnitudes.
Solid arrows = how instructions and data flow; red dashed = flush and refetch after a branch mispredict; grey dashed = coherence messages between cores.
guesses where the next instruction is
reads code from L1I at the predicted
address; a wrong path is thrown away
L2 512 KiB · 8-way (private to the core, code and data)
Caches and memory move data in whole 64 B cache lines
#2 · #6 how many lines one access touches
MESI: one writer or many readers
One cache line can have a copy in several cores' L1/L2.
To write it, a core must first invalidate the others.
#2 false sharing (two cores fight over a line)
#4 cached cursor · #5 more readers, costlier writes
#6 alignas(64) gives an object its own line
Every core has its own L1 and L2
(and its own TLB and store buffer)
another core wants to write a line: invalidations land in core 0's invalidate queue
Memory controller: spreads consecutive addresses across channels (interleaving)
#6 channel balance (line count coprime with channel count)
A bank = a table of rows × columns
Row buffer: the row now open
its own cores, L3, controller and memory
remote memory goes over the interconnect
#1 NUMA: thread and memory on the same node
#1 steer IRQs away from hot cores
(an OS layer, not a cache layer)
The fields of one address (4 KiB pages, L1D 32 KiB 8-way, 64 B lines)
Huge pages: fewer page numbers, fit in the TLB
Page offset bits 0–11 don't change in translation, so L1 picks the set while the TLB translates (VIPT)
→ L1's sets × line size is capped at 4 KiB; it can only grow by adding ways
Cycles assume about 4 GHz. Each level down is roughly 3–10× slower.
Numbers are magnitudes for intuition, not any specific machine.
The map grows with the series: new hardware layers get labels as later posts cover them.
